summary: Martian Map is a planning and rehearsal tool for a human walk (EVA) in Jezero Crater, built on real NASA data. The first people on Mars will leave their habitat with no GPS, a hard suit-time limit, and terrain they have only seen from orbit. Martian Map turns NASA orbital height maps and photos into a 20 m terrain grid and finds the fastest walk through stations where the Perseverance rover actually stood, avoiding ground steeper than the crew's slope limit. It reports time, distance, energy and radiation dose, gives a GO / CAUTION / NO-GO verdict with its reason, and shows where to turn back. Without GPS, position is tracked from base with a growing uncertainty ring until the crew confirms a landmark. Crews can explore the whole crater in 3D, stand on the ground in a simulated view, and switch to a plain EVA screen for outside. Every number shows its unit and source.
details:
What it does: Martian Map plans and rehearses one Mars walk in Jezero Crater. A crew member sees the walk's stations on a map, gets a route that avoids steep ground, and learns whether the walk fits the time limit and where to turn back. It is for planning in the habitat, not mission-critical use.

How it works: A Python pipeline (GDAL, rasterio, pyproj, numpy) clips NASA's MRO CTX height map (20 m) and photo mosaic (5 m) to an 8 x 6 km walk box, derives slope, and builds map layers: satellite, relief, topo, elevation, a CRISM mineral map and the USGS geologic map. Stations come from Perseverance's own waypoints (the Three Forks sample depot, the delta front, its first coring sites), each with the rover's raw photos, and surface conditions come from its MEDA weather station. In the browser (React, MapLibre GL JS, three.js), a route finder in a Web Worker runs Dijkstra on the 20 m grid with a hiking-speed model scaled to Apollo walking speeds and a user-set slope limit. It reports time, distance, energy, radiation dose and a GO / CAUTION / NO-GO verdict. A walk-home time for every point gives the turn-back point and 30/60/90-minute lines.

Creative choices: no-GPS positioning (base as origin, growing uncertainty, landmark fixes), a simulated ground-level view you can walk through, 3D terrain of the whole crater, a large-type EVA mode, field notes and a printable route card.

Honesty and limits: every number shows its unit and source; simulated views and positions are labelled; rocks are too small to see from orbit, so slope stands in for them; the radiation rate is Curiosity's Gale crater measurement applied to Jezero.

Benefits and impact: crews and planners can rehearse a walk on real terrain before stepping outside, and students can see how a Mars EVA is planned. The same pipeline can be pointed at other sites.

Code: https://github.com/talhaarich/mareekh (README explains setup).

Use of AI: AI coding assistants (Claude, via Claude Code and claude.ai) helped write, review and test code and documents; the team reviewed, tested and merged every change. The demo voiceover was generated with AI text-to-speech . No AI-generated images or NASA branding.
dataRefs: Mars 2020 TRN CTX DTM mosaic, 20 m (MRO CTX)
Jezero CTX orthophoto mosaic, 5 m (MRO CTX)
Mars 2020 MEDA weather data (PDS Atmospheres Node)
projectRefs: USGS geologic map of Jezero crater (SIM 3464)
CRISM-based mineral map of Jezero (Parente et al., Zenodo)
